content: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is a hereditary auto-inflammatory disorder that predominantly affects populations in the Mediterranean region. Early research has suggested that colchicine may help prevent FMF attacks. For individuals who are resistant to or intolerant of colchicine, alternative treatments such as anakinra, rilonacept, canakinumab, etanercept, infliximab, or adalimumab may offer potential benefits. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various interventions for reducing inflammation in FMF, updating the previous review published in 2018. The review included 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 312 participants aged 3 to 53 years. These studies assessed interventions such as oral colchicine, ImmunoGuard (a herbal dietary supplement), and subcutaneous injections of rilonacept, anakinra, or canakinumab. The duration of the study arms ranged from one to eight months. While some older colchicine studies had design limitations, the studies on ImmunoGuard, rilonacept, anakinra, and canakinumab were generally well-designed. Colchicine (Oral) vs. Placebo A study using colchicine 0.6 mg three times daily over three months suggested it may reduce the number of individuals experiencing FMF attacks (risk ratio [RR] 0.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 0.95; low-certainty evidence). Another study using colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily over two months found no significant difference in the number of participants experiencing attacks (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.23; low-certainty evidence). There was no clear evidence of differences in the duration of attacks or the interval between attacks (very low-certainty evidence). Adverse effects included loose stools, frequent bowel movements, and diarrhea, but the evidence was of very low certainty. No data were available on acute-phase response markers. Rilonacept vs. Placebo Rilonacept likely does not reduce the number of individuals experiencing attacks at three months (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.26; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no clear evidence of differences in the duration of attacks or the interval between attacks (low-certainty evidence). Adverse effects, including gastrointestinal symptoms, hypertension, headache, respiratory infections, injection site reactions, and herpes, were likely similar between rilonacept and placebo (low-certainty evidence). Acute-phase response markers were likely unaffected after three months (low-certainty evidence). ImmunoGuard vs. Placebo The study on ImmunoGuard found no significant differences in adverse effects or acute-phase response markers after one month of treatment (moderate-certainty evidence). No data were reported on the number of individuals experiencing attacks, the duration of attacks, or the interval between attacks. Anakinra vs. Placebo In a study involving 25 colchicine-resistant participants, anakinra likely did not reduce the number of individuals experiencing attacks at four months (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.07; moderate-certainty evidence). No data were available on the duration of attacks or the interval between attacks. Adverse effects, including injection site reactions, headache, presyncope, dyspnea, and itching, were likely similar between anakinra and placebo (moderate-certainty evidence). Anakinra likely reduced C-reactive protein (CRP) levels after four months (moderate-certainty evidence). Canakinumab vs. Placebo Canakinumab likely reduced the number of individuals experiencing attacks at 16 weeks (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65; moderate-certainty evidence). No data were available on the duration of attacks or the interval between attacks. The rate of serious adverse events was likely lower with canakinumab (42.7 events per 100 patient-years) compared to placebo (97.4 events per 100 patient-years) in colchicine-resistant FMF participants (moderate-certainty evidence). Canakinumab likely resulted in a higher proportion of participants achieving a CRP level of 10 mg/L or less compared to placebo (68% vs. 6%; moderate-certainty evidence). Colchicine Single Dose vs. Divided Dose There was likely no difference in the duration of attacks at three months (mean difference [MD] −0.04 hours, 95% CI −10.91 to 10.83) or six months (MD 2.80 hours, 95% CI −5.39 to 10.99; moderate-certainty evidence). No data were available on the number of individuals experiencing attacks or the interval between attacks. Adverse effects, including anorexia, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and elevated liver enzymes, were likely similar between single-dose and divided-dose regimens (moderate-certainty evidence). There was no clear evidence of differences in acute-phase response markers (lowto moderate-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions The evidence from RCTs evaluating interventions for FMF is limited. Colchicine taken three times daily may reduce the number of individuals experiencing attacks, while single-dose and divided-dose regimens may not differ significantly in efficacy for children with FMF. Canakinumab likely reduces the number of attacks and CRP levels in colchicine-resistant participants. Anakinra may also reduce CRP levels in colchicine-resistant individuals. However, further RCTs are needed to comprehensively assess the efficacy and safety of these and other interventions for FMF.
